content: The iodine value, also referred to as the iodine adsorption value or iodine number, is a chemical parameter that quantifies the mass of iodine, in grams, that reacts with 100 grams of a given chemical substance. Iodine solutions are typically yellow or brown in color, and when a chemical group within the substance reacts with iodine, the color of the solution disappears at a specific concentration. The amount of iodine solution required to maintain the yellow or brown coloration serves as an indicator of the quantity of iodine-reactive groups present in the substance. One significant application of the iodine value is in assessing the degree of unsaturation in fatty acids. This is because the double bonds in unsaturated fatty acids readily react with iodine compounds. A higher iodine value indicates a greater number of unsaturated bonds in the fat or oil being analyzed. In a standard analytical procedure, the fatty acid sample is treated with an excess of Hanus solution, which is a solution containing iodobromine (BrI). Any unreacted iodobromine is subsequently reacted with potassium iodide, which converts it into iodine. The concentration of iodine is then determined through titration using sodium thiosulfate. Established methods for this analysis include ASTM D1959-97 and DIN 53241. For a simplified analysis, 0.2 grams of the fat sample is mixed with 20 cm³ of Wij's solution and 10 cm³ of 1,1,1-trichloroethane. This mixture is left in the dark for 30 minutes to allow the reaction to occur. Following this, 15 cm³ of a 10% potassium iodide solution and 10 cm³ of deionized water are added to the mixture. The resulting solution is then titrated with a 0.1 M sodium thiosulfate (VI) solution. Each 1 cm³ of 0.1 M sodium thiosulfate solution corresponds to 0.01269 grams of iodine. The difference between the titration volume of a control sample (without fat) and the titration volume of the sample containing fat, multiplied by this conversion factor, provides the mass of iodine absorbed by the fat or oil.
